_validation_note: All five candidates fetched and verbatim quotes verified live. Candidate A passed all six gates cleanly. Candidate B passed all six gates but is marginal on Gate 6 (proximity to NO. 01 LNG narrative) and its primary counter-evidence requires a back-of-envelope capacity calculation rather than a single confirmable datum. Candidate A selected as most load-bearing with the strongest, most directly confirmable primary-source rebuttal. Candidates C, D, and E dropped on circulation or steelman grounds.

selected_claim.claim_verbatim: Think on average, we are 30 degrees cooler than Texas, which, when you look at your PUE math, could save a one-gigawatt plant upwards of $150 million a year
selected_claim.claim_paraphrase_fair: Alaska's cold climate gives data center operators a large and quantifiable cooling cost advantage — on the order of $150 million per year for a 1 GW facility — making the state economically competitive for hyperscale AI compute despite its remote location.

asserters.name: Mike Dunleavy
asserters.outlet: Data Center Knowledge (sourced from Data Center World keynote)

selected_claim.steelman: Cold climates genuinely reduce the energy required for data center cooling. Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) is a well-established industry metric, and colder ambient temperatures do lower it — data centers in Iceland and Norway routinely achieve PUEs near 1.1 compared to 1.5 or higher in warm climates. Alaska being significantly cooler than Texas is a physical fact, and free-air cooling eliminates the need for energy-intensive mechanical chillers for much or all of the year. At scale, any reduction in PUE translates to meaningful avoided energy cost, and the directional logic — that Alaska's climate confers a real cooling advantage — is correct. It is entirely reasonable for a governor pitching his state to investors to lead with this advantage.
selected_claim.corrective_thesis: UAF ACEP primary research shows cooling represents only about 5% of total data center operating costs, meaning the $150M figure either requires implausibly large total O&M assumptions or overstates the cooling fraction by an order of magnitude — and Alaska's electricity rates, among the highest in the US at 14-17 cents per kWh versus 6-9 cents in competitor states, create an energy cost disadvantage that structurally dwarfs any cooling savings.

counter_evidence.fact: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power researchers found that 'cooling costs typically represent 5% or less of ongoing operations and maintenance costs' for data centers, directly undermining the scale of the $150M cooling-savings claim.

The same UAF ACEP analysis states: 'Alaska's cost of electricity is among the highest in the U.S.' — a cost headwind on the 40-50% of data center O&M attributable to electricity that overwhelms any cooling-side savings.

Chugach Electric Association stated: 'We currently do not have gas to serve a large data center' — meaning the power infrastructure precondition for any cooling-savings scenario is absent at Alaska's largest grid.

selected_claim.industry_consequence: Hyperscalers and DoD contractors evaluating the Air Force's May 29 2026 JBER/Eielson/Clear lease proposals may accept the $150M cooling headline at face value and underweight Alaska's 14-17 cents per kWh electricity rate — the actual binding cost driver — leading to mispriced bids or misallocated capital in a live, time-sensitive procurement.
